overview.text: Ernest Hemingway’s *A Farewell to Arms* (1929) is a novel set on the Italian front during World War I. Its narrator, American ambulance volunteer Lieutenant Frederic Henry, looks back on his wartime experience and love for English nurse Catherine Barkley. Their relationship unfolds amid injury, military retreat, and loss. The novel draws on Hemingway’s own service as an ambulance driver and wartime injury, but its characters and events are fictionalized rather than a literal memoir. Its significance lies in joining a tragic love story to an unsentimental portrayal of war; Hemingway’s spare, restrained prose lets readers infer much that is left unstated.

key_facts.text: Frederic Henry is an American serving with an ambulance unit in Italy; Catherine Barkley is an English nurse he meets during the war.
Hemingway’s ambulance service and injury in Italy informed the novel, but its story is described as fictionalized and semiautobiographical—not as a direct account of his life.
The National Archives describes the novel as a critique of war’s glorifying language and notes that its tragedy is not simply caused by combat.
Hemingway’s short, restrained prose and omissions—often associated with his “iceberg” approach—are key features of the novel’s style.
